Xinjiang cotton outsmarts extreme heat, external pressure via greater resilience-Xinhua
Xinjiang cotton outsmarts extreme heat, external pressure via greater resilience
Source: Xinhua
Editor: huaxia
2026-10-31 19:23:15
URUMQI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- In a 66.7-hectare demonstration cotton field in Changji, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the average seed cotton yield reached a record high of 9 tonnes per hectare this year.
This would be a strong harvest in any year. It is even more striking as Xinjiang just experienced the hottest summer since 1961. In northern Xinjiang, cotton fields endured 26 days of sustained high temperatures during the critical flowering and boll-setting stage, conditions that would normally cause a plunge in output.
Statistics from the China Cotton Association (CCA) put China's cotton planting area in 2026 at 43.054 million mu (about 2.87 million hectares), down 3.9 percent, with an estimated yield of 166.2 kilograms per mu, up 0.5 percent. Meanwhile, Xinjiang's cotton yield is expected to reach 173.8 kilograms per mu, higher than the national average. The region's total output is estimated to account for 95.9 percent of the national total, further consolidating Xinjiang's role as the "ballast" of China's cotton production.
How has the Xinjiang cotton industry maintained stable, high output despite the combined pressure of extreme weather, persistent "forced labor" disinformation and external sanctions? Xinhua reporters recently visited cotton fields, factory floors and an industry forum to explore what makes the local cotton industry so resilient.
SMART COTTON FIELDS
Song Meizhen, chief scientist of the high-quality cotton team at the western agricultural research center of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said the prolonged heat during this year's flowering and boll-setting stage created enormous stress. However, on-site yield measurement by an expert group showed the demonstration field surpassed 600 kilograms per mu, thanks to an integrated technology model combining good seeds, appropriate methods and suitable machinery.
The demonstration field is part of a smart cotton field jointly built by the Changji National Agricultural High-tech Industry Demonstration Zone and the research center, where weather stations, soil moisture sensors, inspection robots and drones form an integrated air-space-ground monitoring network.
The cotton varieties selected were high-quality, high-yield and multi-resistant lines such as Zhongmian 113. Sensors, notably, collected field data around the clock to enable precise water and fertilizer regulation.
Especially in June, July and August, when temperatures exceeded 35 degrees Celsius for nearly 30 days, the intelligent water-fertilizer integrated control system switched irrigation to low-volume, high-frequency water supply, reducing bud and boll shedding caused by heat and drought, Song said.
The flowering and boll-setting stage is critical for yield formation: high temperatures can disrupt pollination and cause shedding. In this smart cotton field, however, experience-based farming has been turned into data-based farming, allowing more timely and targeted responses to mitigate possible negative impacts.
This year, building on a green and intelligent cotton cultivation system developed over the past two years, the field further integrated cotton data with a production decision-making model, introduced plant-protection robots, and applied Internet of Things to deliver water and fertilizer. As a result, fertilizer use efficiency rose by 20 to 30 percent, while water consumption dropped by more than 30 percent.
Li Guozhao, a veteran cotton farmer, recalled that 36 years ago, he planted 15 mu of cotton. At that time, he cut cotton stalks by hand, irrigated the land by flooding, topped plants manually and hired pickers. By season's end, his hands were often covered with blood blisters.
Today, his 350 mu of cotton requires only two hired workers. Drone-based plant protection and machine picking cost as low as 160 yuan (about 23.83 U.S. dollars) to 180 yuan per mu. His next step is to install smart valves for irrigation, so he can water the fields via a tap on his phone.
The United States' so-called "Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act" took effect in 2022, and has since disrupted Xinjiang cotton exports to the U.S. market. "But the U.S. sanctions have had no impact on me," Li said.
In Xinjiang, the traditional hoe known locally as a khetman has long been replaced by Beidou satellite navigation, just as hand-picking cotton has made way for machine harvesting, leaving no ground for the "forced labor" narrative.
Across Xinjiang, a "super cotton field" project featuring extremely high unmanned operation rates in management had been extended to over 2 million mu by the end of 2025.
At present, the comprehensive mechanization rate for cotton cultivation and harvesting in Xinjiang has reached 97 percent, with machine-picking accounting for over 90 percent.
FULL-INDUSTRIAL-CHAIN STRENGTH
Resilience does not only grow in the fields. It extends into factory workshops.
Xinjiang is promoting local processing of the entire chain from planting, ginning and spinning to weaving, dyeing and garment-making. In 2025, the share of cotton processed locally reached 45 percent. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the region plans to continue developing industries of high-count combed yarn, home textiles and technical textiles.
In southern Xinjiang, Aksu and Bayingolin have laid out million-spindle intelligent spinning bases, while Kashgar and Hotan are taking on apparel and home-textile manufacturing. Dyeing and finishing operations are being concentrated in industrial parks for low-carbon upgrades.
In digital factories, intelligent cotton blending, automated transfer and real-time management systems are already online.
On April 10, an express train loaded with 1,118 tonnes of cotton departed from Bachu Station in Xinjiang for Zibo in east China's Shandong Province, which is 4,600 kilometers away. The entire lifespan of each cotton bale, from field picking and factory processing to rail transport, was recorded by Internet of Things systems. A receiving company can scan a code to see which Xinjiang cotton field the bale came from, which production line it passed through, and what temperature and humidity changes it experienced on the train.
Xinjiang, as China's "cotton granary," has continued to improve cotton output and quality in recent years and consolidate its advantage in large-scale farming, said Liang Yong, a national political advisor and director of the Xinjiang cotton industry development leading group office.
At the 2026 Xinjiang Cotton and Yarn Industry Development Forum held on Sept. 9, Liang noted that the region's textile and apparel industry has risen markedly in the national industrial landscape, with segments such as yarn, grey fabric and chemical fiber accelerating into the front ranks.
Originally aimed at blocking Xinjiang cotton from the U.S. market, sanctions have instead sped up the creation of a self-sufficient green manufacturing system. Sustainable cotton standards, low-carbon accounting and better quality for better prices are gradually taking hold. As experts at the forum noted, the more integrated the industrial chain becomes, the weaker the impact from any single-point blockade.
False narratives can be repeated and sanctions can be escalated, but truth will prevail, as the thriving cotton industry in Xinjiang attests. Here, season after season of high yields have shown that what sanctions cannot touch is an agricultural system successfully integrating technology, land, people and the industrial chain.
Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security announced that it had added three Chinese entities to the so-called "Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List," which China strongly condemns and firmly opposes.
The U.S. measures have no factual basis, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce said, accusing the U.S. side of persistently manipulating human rights issues to pursue unilateral protectionism and bullying under the guise of human rights protection.
In an earlier statement, the CCA said the true intent behind such a move is to politicize and weaponize human rights issues in an attempt to contain the development of China's cotton and textile industries, while such actions will also undermine the stability of global cotton industrial chains.
China's cotton industry has the confidence and capabilities to overcome challenges posed by external pressure, it said, noting that China has the world's most complete cotton and textile industrial chains, a vast domestic consumer market, and an increasingly diversified international market layout. ■

Cyclonic storm may hit Andhra Pradesh coast on November 3
IMD Director General Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said the possible cyclonic storm could bring wind speeds of 80 kmph to 90 kmph, with occasional gusts reaching 100 kmph."The wind speed of the possible cyclonic storm is likely to be between 80 kmph and 90 kmph, with occasional gusts up to 100 kmph. It may make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast on Tuesday morning," Mohapatra said.
In its bulletin issued at 3 pm on Saturday, the weather department said the well-marked low-pressure area over the Southeast Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Andaman Sea had intensified into a depression.
The system concentrated into a depression at 11.30 am on October 31 over the same region, the IMD said.
Depression likely to intensify into deep depression, cyclonic storm
According to the IMD, the depression was located around 330 km west-southwest of Sri Vijayapuram in the Andaman Islands and 300 km west-northwest of Car Nicobar.The weather system is likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify into a deep depression over the Southeast Bay of Bengal during the next 12 hours.
"Continuing to move west-northwestwards, it is very likely to intensify further into a cyclonic storm over southeast and adjoining areas of southwest and West-central Bay of Bengal during the subsequent 12 hours and reach over West-central Bay of Bengal near Andhra Pradesh coast around evening of November 2," the bulletin said.
A depression is a weather system that is stronger than a low-pressure area but less intense than a cyclonic storm.
IMD monitors system, forecasts rain in Odisha
The IMD is tracking the system's movement and has said it will issue further updates as it develops.The director of the Meteorological Centre in Bhubaneswar, Manorama Mohanty, said, "We are monitoring the system's progress and will issue further updates as it evolves."
The weather department has also forecast light to moderate rain or thundershowers in a few districts of Odisha.

Demonstrating its commitment to the welfare of the people, the Nevis Island Administration (NIA) Cabinet continues to explore possible electricity relief measures to ease the financial burden on consumers amid rising global fuel costs
Speaking at his monthly press conference on October 27, Premier of Nevis and Minister of Finance, Public Utilities, and Energy et al. in the Nevis Island Administration, the Honourable Mark Brantley, explained that the high cost of electricity stems from external factors beyond the government’s control. The surge in fuel prices has contributed to significant increases in energy costs across the globe, in some cases, resulting in increases of more than 60 percent.
Premier Brantley disclosed that the government is examining a proposal developed by the Nevis Electricity Company Limited (NEVLEC) to determine what temporary relief could be provided to consumers as the island’s finances stabilise with the start of the tourism season.
“The high cost of electricity in Nevis is due to external circumstances, but I’ve made the commitment that as we hope our finances stabilize as the tourism season kicks off, that we will see what is possible. Already I know that we have a proposal that NEVLEC has developed so that we can work out what relief we can bring on a temporary basis. I want to emphasize that -on a temporary basis- to the people of Nevis.”
The Premier acknowledged the financial pressures facing households and expressed sympathy for residents struggling to meet basic needs, including those forced to choose between paying their electricity bills and purchasing food.
“To see the electricity bill double has really created significant difficulty. I don’t want the public at any point to think that I am somehow unaware of or immune to that. I live in my community. I talk to people in my community. I understand the pain that people are enduring. We need to do something about it. The problem that we have had is our capacity to do something about it, because the government simply could not continue to swallow the fuel surcharge as we had done for the last four years. The Strait of Hormuz situation which even now continues, that has been our reality and that is our lived reality and we now have to deal with it. But we must fashion a solution and we must find some way to provide some relief and I give that commitment that we are working on it.”
Premier Brantley further explained that any relief measures would be designed to prioritise the welfare of the most vulnerable members of society, with particular consideration for low-energy users, including pensioners and persons on fixed incomes who are struggling financially.
Before the fuel surcharge was reintroduced in July 2026, the NIA had absorbed millions of dollars in fuel costs by removing the surcharge from consumers’ electricity bills for four years. However, the continued rise in global fuel prices and the government’s financial constraints have made it necessary to reassess how best to support consumers while meeting its financial obligations.

Heat advisory issued for several parts of Sri Lanka on Sunday
October 31, 2026 at
4:16 PM
The Department of Meteorology has issued an amber-level warm weather advisory for several parts of Sri Lanka, warning of increased heat conditions on Sunday (November 1).
According to the Natural Hazards Early Warning Centre, the heat index, or the temperature felt by the human body, is expected to rise to the ‘Caution’ level in some areas of the North-Central, Eastern and North-Western provinces, as well as the Mannar and Vavuniya districts.
The advisory, issued at 4.00 p.m. on Saturday (31), warns that the elevated heat index is likely to be experienced during daytime hours.
Residents in the affected areas are advised to take precautions against prolonged exposure to heat, including staying hydrated, taking breaks in shaded areas and limiting strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest parts of the day.
The heat index reflects how hot conditions feel to the human body when air temperature and relative humidity are combined.
The advisory is valid for November 1, 2026. (Newswire)
